payload.title: Present Day
payload.blurb: Toledo, Ohio, late November 2026. You finished college in May, moved back into your mother's house in Point Place, and still have no job. A one-bedroom lease in the Old West End starts in three weeks. Tomorrow morning a freight company in Louisville wants you in a chair for an interview, six hours…
payload.overview: Present-day Toledo, Ohio, a city of about 270,000 people on the Maumee River where it meets Lake Erie. Toledo built itself on glass, then on cars and the freight that moves between them, and it still runs on shifts: the downtown hospitals, the state offices, the auto plant on the north side, and the diners that open before the sun is up. The people are ordinary Americans, mostly from families who came from Poland, Slovakia, Germany, Ireland, the rural South and Mexico, with newer neighbors from everywhere. Phones, cars, banks and job boards all work the way they do anywhere else. There are no levels, classes or status windows here. Nothing in the city runs on magic, and nothing is coming to end it. Life moves slowly here. Work comes through relatives and neighbors, a lease is a promise written on paper, and a bad winter can make a decision for you. Most people stay within an hour of where they were raised, and the ones who leave are talked about at every Sunday meal.
payload.intro: The kitchen light is the only one on in the house on Point Place, and the furnace has just come on for the first time this season. It is a little after nine on a Tuesday night in late November, and the wind off the lake keeps pressing against the storm windows. An interview letter from Tri-River Logistics is folded in half beside the sugar bowl, with the Louisville address printed across the top. Denise Wojcik sits at the table in her hospital fleece, a plate of cold pierogi in front of her that she has not touched, her lanyard still around her neck from a double shift that ended at seven. She has not said the word Louisville since you came in, and the silence has weight of its own. Your phone is face down by the napkin holder, and it has buzzed twice since dinner. Denise looks at the phone, then at you, and waits.
starters: Bea's Counter opened at six, and by a quarter past the front window is already fogged from the coffee urn and the flat-top. It is Saturday in late November, the sky over Lagrange Street still dark, and the regulars sit where they have sat for twenty years. Bea Whitfield stands behind the counter in a black apron, refilling a coffee pot with one hand and holding a clipboard in the other, a pen clipped above her ear. Two weekend breakfast shifts have opened since the last cook quit, and she has been looking at the empty stool at the end of the counter like it owes her money. The chalkboard by the register still has your name on it from the week you bussed tables last summer. Bea taps the empty stool with the clipboard and keeps one hand on the pot, waiting to see whether you take it.

The storefront on Lagrange Street has been dark for four years, and the window still carries the faded gold lettering of a tavern that closed before Danny Szymanski was old enough to drink there. It is Sunday afternoon, the light already going low over the rooftops, and the air inside smells of old grease and cold concrete. A stainless steel commercial hood hangs over the back line, scarred and clean. Walt Szymanski sits on an overturned milk crate by the door with his hearing aid turned off, a folder of papers on his knee. Danny stands near the hood with his phone in one hand, flour still on his forearms from a morning shift, and a napkin sketch of a pierogi truck in the other. The papers in the folder need a signature by Friday. Walt has not picked up the pen, and Danny has stopped talking.

The gate lights on the east side of the Jeep plant are the brightest thing on the block at a quarter to six on a Thursday morning. Third shift is ending and first shift is pulling in, and the lot is packed with pickups and thermoses steaming in the cold. The air tastes of metal and diesel, and somewhere inside a horn sounds twice and goes quiet. Kenya Mott leans against the door of her car in a Carhartt jacket with the sleeves pushed up, a reflective vest over one shoulder, her braids under a knit cap. Her coffee has gone cold in the cup holder, and she has been standing here since five. She says she has news about a form, and she is watching your face to see whether you already know what it says.

entries.title: Your start
entries.content: You are 22, a graduate who finished your degree in May and has been living in your mother's house in Point Place since August with no job lined up. A one-bedroom lease in the Old West End starts in three weeks. Tomorrow morning you have an interview for an analyst job in Louisville, six hours away.

entries.title: Factions
entries.content:
Tri-River Logistics - a Louisville freight firm with one analyst seat open and a manager who wants someone who can move in January.
Toledo Assembly Complex - the Jeep plant on the north side, a union line that hires in waves and wants people who show up.
The Lagrange Street families - the north side's Polish and Slovak families, who keep their cousins' jobs, recipes and opinions in the same place.
The downtown hospitals - the largest employers after the state, always short of staff and quick to hire anyone who can start in two weeks.

entries.title: Toledo in brief
entries.content: Toledo is a city of about 270,000 people in northwest Ohio, where the Maumee River meets Lake Erie. It is called the Glass City for the bottle and window glass that built it. Everything here is ordinary: phones, cars, job boards, hospital shifts, and winters that come off the lake. Nothing magic happens, and nothing is coming to end it. The city is slow to change and quick to talk about who left.

entries.title: How work gets found
entries.content: Jobs here are found through people, not websites. A cousin hears of an opening, a neighbor puts in a word, a nurse knows the floor manager. Applications still go online, but the call that matters usually comes from someone who knows someone. Big employers hire in waves, and a start date often falls two or three weeks after an offer. Lease dates and job dates rarely line up, and that is where most plans tangle.

entries.title: Point Place
entries.content: Point Place is a neighborhood on the northwest side of Toledo, where the land runs out toward Maumee Bay. Small brick and frame houses sit on narrow lots, and some streets end in a view of the water and the marsh. The wind off the lake is hard in November. The family houses here have finished basements, porches that need paint, and kitchen tables that have seen every argument since the nineties.

entries.title: Old West End
entries.content: The Old West End is a historic district just north of downtown, full of big Victorian and Queen Anne houses, most of them cut into apartments. Maples line the streets, and a few corner bakeries and bars keep going on foot traffic. Apartments here go quickly in spring and sit empty through winter. Landlords expect the first and last month paid on time, and a lease start date is firm, so a late move costs more than the rent.

entries.title: Tri-River Logistics
entries.content: Tri-River Logistics is a freight broker with an office on the Ohio River in Louisville, about six hours south of Toledo by interstate. It moves loads between plants, warehouses and carriers, and it has one open seat for an operations analyst who tracks lanes and bad shipments. Pam Ostrander runs operations and hires by phone first. She wants someone who will move by January, answers at seven, and does not need the job explained twice.

entries.title: Names
entries.content: Names in Toledo follow the families who came to it. North side names are often Polish, Slovak, Hungarian or German, with long surnames that get shortened at work. East side names are often Black Toledo families with roots in the Southern migration and the auto plants, or Irish and Scottish. South end names are often Mexican or Puerto Rican. Given names are common and plain, such as Denise, Danny, Kenya or Walt. Newer neighbors bring names from everywhere, and nobody thinks that is strange.

entries.title: Lagrange Street
entries.content: Lagrange Street runs through the north side and holds old Polish and Slovak parishes, bakeries, bars, and the fish fries that run on Friday nights in Lent. Families here keep the same storefronts for decades. A shuttered storefront with a commercial hood and an old tavern kitchen is a rare find, and the owners who still hold them tend to be older relatives who say no for a long time before they say anything else.

entries.title: Bea's Counter
entries.content: Bea's Counter is a twenty-four seat diner on Lagrange Street that opens at six every morning. It serves eggs, soup, pierogi on Fridays and coffee from a pot that is never fully emptied. Bea Whitfield owns it and hires on a one-hour trial at the grill. Weekend and Monday breakfast shifts open up in the cold months, when some regulars stop coming in for coffee.

entries.title: Glass City history
entries.content: Toledo's glass industry began in the late 1800s, when natural gas drew bottle and window glass makers to the city. Libbey and the bottle makers employed generations of families, and the glass money built many of the houses, churches and streets people still live in. The factories shrank over the decades, and the city has argued ever since about what should replace them. Old glass still shows up in antique shops and church windows.

entries.title: Toledo Assembly Complex
entries.content: The Toledo Assembly Complex is the Jeep plant on the north side, one of the biggest employers in the city. It runs three shifts, and second shift goes past midnight. The union line hires in waves when orders come in. Families on the north side usually have someone inside, and a referral from a line worker tends to get an application read first.

entries.title: Pierogi as business
entries.content: Pierogi are a small, real business here. Church kitchens sell them by the dozen, a few frozen brands sell to grocery stores in Ohio and Michigan, and food trucks fry them with onions outside breweries after lunch. Starting a food business means a licensed commercial kitchen, a health inspection, a food handler card for every cook, and a buyer who will pay before the product spoils. Most people who try it run it on the side first.

entries.title: The downtown hospitals
entries.content: The downtown hospitals are the largest employers after the state and the university. They run short-staffed, with nurses and respiratory therapists on twelve hour shifts, nights and weekends. A hospital job can start within two weeks, which makes it the easy answer families hope for. Night rotations pay a differential, and people who work them tend to swap stories about the same few patients.

entries.title: Job interviews here
entries.content: A job interview for an office role here usually means a phone screen, then one or two in-person rounds over a few weeks. Companies that want you in person often cover part of the travel and expect you to pay the rest. A job offer comes with a start date, and that date often arrives before the lease does. Recruiters call the number on the application, and a missed call can end a process before it starts.

entries.title: The drive south
entries.content: The drive from Toledo to Louisville runs south on the interstate through Ohio farmland to Cincinnati, then across into Kentucky, about six hours in good weather. In late November the open stretches can turn to whiteout within minutes, and trucks stack up at the exits. Gas stations along the route are dependable, but you need a full tank before you leave.

entries.title: Lake Erie weather
entries.content: Lake Erie makes its own weather. From November to March the wind comes off the water cold and wet, clouds sit low over the shore, and the first real snow usually lands in December. People who grew up here dress for it and do not talk about it much. A forty degree day feels colder near the water, and the marsh by the bay freezes at the edges first.

world.vibe: Quiet, gray and specific, with the family table as the loudest room. People say the practical thing and mean the other one.

opening.note: Staged. Beat one: the kitchen on Point Place, the first minute of the scene. Establish the single lit kitchen, the cold coming through the storm windows, the letter from Tri-River beside the sugar bowl, and the plate of pierogi nobody is eating. Denise Wojcik speaks first. She talks about the weather, the hospital schedule and the gas bill before she says anything about Louisville. She wants you home, and she wants it understood without her having to say it. Beat two: the interruption is the phone. Danny's messages keep coming in, a photo of a napkin sketch, then a voice note that starts with okay but listen. Keep them short and loud, and let Denise notice each one without comment. Beat three: by the third turn the player is facing a real choice between the drive south in the morning, a Saturday shift at Bea's counter that would keep you in Toledo, or an evening at the Lagrange storefront with Walt and Danny, where the papers wait for a signature. Hold Kenya's news and the lease paperwork back until the player asks about the apartment or the plant. Let the kitchen stay warm and the silence stay honest.

cast.name: Denise Wojcik
cast.role: Your mother. A respiratory therapist on night rotation at the downtown hospital, who wants you under her roof until something with a steady paycheck and a parking space shows up.
cast.look: Short and broad-shouldered, dark hair dyed a warm brown and pinned back, hospital clogs, and a fleece with her lanyard still on after a double shift.
cast.manner: Speaks in finished sentences and never raises her voice. Says fine when she means the opposite, and switches off the television instead of arguing.
cast.secret: She has already called Tri-River to ask whether they hire people from Toledo who do not want to move, and she has been hoping the answer was no. She has not told you she called.

cast.name: Danny Szymanski
cast.role: Your oldest friend, a line cook on the north side who has been sending business plans at all hours for a pierogi food truck and a frozen goods side line.
cast.look: Lanky, sandy hair under a black beanie, flour on his forearms in every photo, and a chipped front tooth he never got fixed.
cast.manner: Talks in bursts, then goes quiet and waits for you to say it is insane. Starts nearly every pitch with okay but listen, and laughs at his own jokes before anyone else can.
cast.secret: He already paid a deposit on cleaning the storefront's commercial hood with money his grandfather lent him, and he has not told Walt that the money was spent.

cast.name: Pam Ostrander
cast.role: Operations manager at Tri-River Logistics in Louisville, running tomorrow's interview for the analyst seat, with little patience for anyone who wastes her time.
cast.look: Tall, with reading glasses pushed up into short gray-blond hair, a navy blazer, a silver lanyard, and a phone that never stops buzzing on the desk.
cast.manner: Clipped and precise. Ends calls before you expect them to end and reads her questions off a printed form. Takes notes on the back of a printed resume and never writes down what you say.
cast.secret: The analyst seat was already offered to another candidate, who turned it down last week, so tomorrow's interview is only there to fill the second chair. She has already decided whether she likes you.

cast.name: Gene Lubinski
cast.role: Owns the Old West End building where your one-bedroom lease starts in three weeks. He lives in the first-floor unit and keeps the old dry cleaner's storefront locked and full of boxes.
cast.look: Thick forearms, a Mud Hens windbreaker zipped to the chin, reading glasses on a cord, and a limp from a bad knee he will not talk about.
cast.manner: Slow and friendly. Repeats the rent in full so nobody can say later they did not hear it, and says we'll see the way other people say no.
cast.secret: He has already listed your unit for January to a couple who offered more money, and he is waiting to see whether you sign the lease he mailed before he tells you.

cast.name: Bea Whitfield
cast.role: Owns Bea's Counter, a diner on Lagrange Street that opens at six, and needs someone for weekend and Monday breakfast shifts before the cold months empty out the regulars.
cast.look: Small and quick, silver hair in a claw clip, a black apron over a church rummage sale sweatshirt, and reading glasses she wears on top of her head and forgets.
cast.manner: Asks how your feet are before she says anything about work. Wipes the same six inches of counter while she talks, and never says thank you, only there you go.
cast.secret: She is quietly selling the building, and the buyer is a chain that wants the lot. Any hire she makes now is the last one she will make as an owner.

cast.name: Kenya Mott
cast.role: Your friend from the rec center softball team, now a second-shift line worker at the Jeep plant on the north side, who has been trying to get you on there for months.
cast.look: Compact and strong, braids pulled back under a knit cap, a Carhartt jacket with the sleeves pushed up, and a reflective vest folded in her bag.
cast.manner: Blunt and fast. Finishes your sentences wrong on purpose and switches from teasing to serious without warning, with no pause in between.
cast.secret: She put your name on a referral form at the plant last month without asking you, and the hiring window closes in January. She has been waiting for the right moment to tell you, and the moment keeps not coming.

cast.name: Arturo Villanueva
cast.role: A reference and job-help librarian at a branch of the Toledo-Lucas County public library on the west side, who runs free resume review on Wednesday evenings and remembers the people who come back.
cast.look: Trim, with a neat beard going gray at the chin, a cardigan with leather elbow patches, and a library badge on a lanyard with a pen clipped to it.
cast.manner: Patient and dry. Makes you read your own bullet points out loud, speaks quietly enough that people lean in, and corrects grammar by reading the sentence back to you slower.
cast.secret: He was laid off from a logistics data job in Louisville five years ago and has never told anyone at the library what he did before. That is why he knows exactly which resumes get read, and why he has been reading yours twice.

cast.name: Walt Szymanski
cast.role: Danny's grandfather, a retired tool and die machinist who owns the empty storefront on Lagrange Street that Danny wants for the pierogi kitchen.
cast.look: Stooped but solid, an army surplus jacket over a wool vest, a white crew cut, a hearing aid he turns off during arguments, and hands with scarred knuckles.
cast.manner: Speaks in short declarative sentences, and tells stories about the old plant that always end in a lesson.
cast.secret: He has been refusing to sign the storefront lease papers because he does not think Danny will still be doing this in a year. He is waiting to see whether you will back his grandson or back him.

systems.label: Direction
systems.meaning: How much your life is pointing at something: a job, a city, a date you can name. Low means you are drifting on your mother's couch.
systems.change: Up when you apply, interview, sign something or lock in a date. Down when a week goes by with nothing moving, or when you let someone else's plan decide for you.

systems.label: Standing with your mother
systems.meaning: How close you are to Denise right now, and how much of her plan for you you are still carrying.
systems.change: Up when you keep a promise, eat at her table, or tell her where you will be. Down when you go quiet, lie about where you are, or leave without saying.

systems.label: The pierogi plan
systems.meaning: Where Danny's food truck idea stands, in a few words.
systems.change: Moves when you visit the Lagrange storefront, talk real numbers with Danny, or tell him no. It starts as a napkin sketch.

npcSystems.label: Trust
npcSystems.meaning: How much this person believes you will do what you say.
npcSystems.change: Up when you keep a small promise to them. Down when you cancel, wave off their advice, or repeat what they told you in confidence.

style.art: Overcast photographic realism in gray and rust, with Lake Erie blue at the edges: brick two-flats, bare maples, a parked sedan under a streetlight, wet sidewalks in late autumn.
style.avoid: Fantasy props, glowing effects, posed portraits and anything that looks like a stock photo of a city.

heroes.name: Sam Kovach
heroes.description: Accounting degree in May, forty-one applications sent, two replies, and a six-hour drive to Louisville in the morning.
heroes.look: Medium height, a wool coat he bought for the interview, short dark hair he cut himself, and a quiet face that gets smaller when he is embarrassed.
heroes.background: Grew up on the east side and worked the register at a grocery store all through school. Got the accounting degree with loans he tries not to think about. He has never lived anywhere but Toledo, and he has never once been asked what he wants.
heroes.carries: A printed resume in a plastic sleeve and a pen from the grocery store.

heroes.name: Lena Marek
heroes.description: Chemistry degree, a grandmother's pierogi recipe, and no clear idea what a chemist does in Toledo.
heroes.look: Tall and freckled, auburn hair in a loose knot, a canvas jacket with paint spots on the cuffs, and nails bitten short.
heroes.background: Raised in the Old West End by a grandmother who ran a bakery on Lagrange Street. Took a lab job in college, hated the solvent smell, and quit the summer before her last year to come home and think. Her grandmother has been gone two years, and the bakery has been gone longer.
heroes.carries: Her grandmother's recipe card for pierogi dough, soft at the corners from handling.

heroes.name: Jules Adeyemi
heroes.description: Urban planning degree and a summer lifeguard job at the Y. Knows which bus routes the city cut and which ones it will cut next.
heroes.look: Slight, close-cropped hair dyed a dark plum, a bike helmet clipped to a worn backpack, and a Metroparks fleece with the zipper broken halfway.
heroes.background: Grew up in Point Place with two moms in a small house near the bay. Did the planning degree in Columbus, wrote a thesis on bus service on the west side, and came home sure the city is already drawing lines without anyone's say.
heroes.carries: A transit map marked up in three colors and a monthly pass for the regional bus system.
